turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, thanks for seeing me. Honestly, I’m not usually the type to go to doctors for every little thing—I mean, I’m a CEO, I built my company from the ground up, didn't even finish high school, so I’m used to just powering through problems, you know? But what made me come in today is that... well, for the past year or so, it’s like I have zero filter for distractions. 

The absolute smallest thing will just completely derail me. I'll be sitting there trying to review a contract, and my phone will give a tiny buzz—not even a ring, just a buzz—and boom, I've dropped everything to look at it. Or somebody will walk past my office. I have these big glass walls, which I thought was a great leadership move, you know, 'open door policy' and all that, but now every time someone from accounting walks by to get a coffee, my attention just snaps right to them before I can even stop it. 

And it’s not even just stuff happening around me, it’s my own brain, too. I’ll be right in the middle of something important and out of nowhere, I’ll get a totally random thought about my in-laws—like wondering what my father-in-law is going to complain about at the next family dinner—and it just pulls me completely off what I’m doing. Before I can even catch myself and tell myself to focus, I've lost my train of thought entirely. It's just getting ridiculous.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being easily derailed by minor external stimuli, such as a phone buzzing or people walking by, as well as by unrelated internal thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: Did you experience similar difficulties with attention and focus when you were a child or in school?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, you know, it’s funny you ask that because... well, looking back, this was definitely around when I was a kid, too. Honestly, school was—well, let’s just say there’s a reason I didn't stick around to get that piece of paper, right? I mean, my teachers... God, it felt like every single week they were moving my seat. It was like a game of musical chairs that only I was playing. Mrs. Gable in fifth grade, Mr. Henderson in eighth, they were always, and I mean absolutely always, moving me around the room. 

They’d put me in the front row so they could keep an eye on me, but then I'd just talk to the teacher. Then they'd move me to the back, and I'd be distracting the kids in the back. Because I just talked too much. I really did, I could hold a conversation with a brick wall. If a thought popped into my head, it was coming out of my mouth right that second. 

And I was always just... getting up. Just standing up and walking around the classroom without asking for permission or raising my hand or anything. I’d just get up to throw a tiny piece of paper away, or look out the window, or just stretch my legs, mainly because sitting in that little plastic chair for forty-five minutes felt physically impossible. 

And the questions! Man, the teachers hated this—I was always blurting things out before they even finished asking the question. A teacher would be halfway through a sentence, like, 'If a train leaves the station at...' and I'm already shouting out the answer before they even get to the end of the math problem. I just couldn't wait. It was like I couldn't hold the words in my mouth. So, yeah, I guess I was definitely a handful back then, too.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes frequently standing up and walking around the classroom without permission when they were expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states they 'talked too much' and could 'hold a conversation with a brick wall.'
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient reports they were 'always blurting things out before they even finished asking the question.'

turns.doctor_question: Do these difficulties with distraction and staying focused affect your life outside of work, such as at home or in your personal relationships?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, I mean, that’s the thing, right? It’s not just the glass walls at the office. I’m still keeping up overall, like, the company isn't going under, the lights are still on at home, but... it’s starting to bleed into everything else. 

Take home, for instance. My wife—she’s incredibly patient, a saint, really, to put up with me all these years—but even she’s getting frustrated. Just last weekend, we were supposed to be having this serious conversation about renovating the kitchen. She’s got the samples out, the whole nine yards, and she’s talking about cabinet finishes. And right in the middle of her sentence, I just... I saw a leaf blower outside the window and suddenly I'm talking about how we need to fire the landscaping company because they always come on Saturdays. And she just looked at me like, 'Are you even in this room right now?' It’s starting to cost me her trust, you know? Like she doesn't believe I'm actually present when we're making family plans or talking about the kids. 

And it’s happening with my team at work, too, in a different way. I do a lot of mentoring—I like to think I’m a pretty hands-on CEO, I want to bring the younger guys up—but lately, those one-on-one conversations are just... a mess. A junior exec will be pouring his heart out about a project hurdle, and I’m just totally zoned out, thinking about whether I responded to an email from three days ago. Or I'll just interrupt them mid-sentence to talk about something completely unrelated. I can see it on their faces. They’re losing patience with me. The meetings don't go the way they should, the mentoring doesn't happen, and I end up looking like I just don't care, which isn't true at all! I care a lot, it's just... I can't stay on the track. So, yeah, it's definitely not just the paperwork that's taking a hit.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient states they 'can't stay on the track' and zone out during conversations, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes zoning out when spoken to directly by his wife and junior executives, making them feel he is not listening.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (a leaf blower) and unrelated thoughts (an old email).
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly mentions interrupting junior executives mid-sentence to talk about unrelated things.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly denies not caring, stating 'I care a lot,' which denies a loss of interest or indifference.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself struggling with persistent, excessive worry about everyday things that feels difficult to control?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly? Not at all. Worry really isn't my thing. I mean, people look at how fast I move and how many plates I'm spinning, and they always assume I must be stressed out of my mind, right? Like, 'Oh, he's running a company, he must be losing sleep over the profit margins or the supply chain or the economy.' But to be completely straight with you, I don't sit around wringing my hands about everyday stuff. If there's a problem, I just tackle it. Boom, done, onto the next thing. 

Like, just last month, we had this massive issue with a major materials vendor. A lot of guys in my position would be sweating bullets, pacing the floor, worrying about the bottom line taking a hit or what the investors would say. But my brain just doesn't work like that. I don't get stuck in that... that endless loop of 'what if this happens, what if that happens.' I just picked up the phone, fired the vendor, found a new one in twenty minutes, and moved on with my day. 

So it's definitely not that I'm distracted because I'm anxious or fretting about things. I'm not worried about the landscaping company when I interrupt my wife, I'm just suddenly fixated on the fact that I need to call them and I want to do it right that exact second. It's always about action with me, not sitting around worrying. I honestly don't even think I have the patience to worry! If you think about it, worrying actually takes a lot of focus. You have to be able to hold onto a single negative thought for a long time to really worry about it, and as we've established, holding onto a single thought for more than a minute is exactly my problem right now! So yeah, no, I'm not a worrier at all.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient states that holding onto a single thought for more than a minute is exactly his problem right now, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes himself as moving fast, spinning many plates, and states 'It's always about action with me', indicating constant activity.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly mentions interrupting his wife when he suddenly thinks of something he needs to do.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies excessive worry, stating 'Worry really isn't my thing' and 'I don't sit around wringing my hands about everyday stuff.'
symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient denies getting stuck in an endless loop of 'what ifs' and states he is not a worrier at all, rejecting uncontrollable worry.
